caption: "greenland" — 100,000+ searches this week. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the island in the deal.

Why: on September 18 Trump posted that the US and Denmark had agreed "permanent control over security" in Greenland at "no cost" to the US, with a large military presence to come. Denmark says Greenland stays Danish, with self-determination written in.

What most people don't know: the US has had a base there since 1951. Pituffik held about 10,000 people at its Cold War peak; about 150 serve there now. In 1946 Washington offered $100 million in gold for the island. Denmark said no.
Very simply put: 56,000 people, one US base, a deal for forever.

slides.headline: Announced September 18: 'permanent control over security', at *no cost*.
slides.sub: Trump's post promised a large military presence. Denmark says Greenland stays Danish, with self-determination written in.

slides.headline: The deal bans *non-NATO* bases and screens Chinese and Russian money.
slides.sub: Permanent US access, basing and overflight rights; it stays in force even if Greenland becomes independent.

slides.headline: The US has had a base there since *1951*.
slides.sub: Pituffik, formerly Thule, 1,210 km north of the Arctic Circle: the northernmost US military installation.
slides.image: A large white radar dome on a flat snowy plain under a pale arctic sky, dome in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain snow, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: Cold War peak: about *10,000* people. Today: about 150.
slides.sub: Built 1951 to 1953 for bombers, now Space Force missile warning and space surveillance.
slides.image: An empty airstrip stretching across snow towards distant icy mountains, runway lights glowing, airstrip in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain snow, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: In 1968 a US bomber crashed there with *four nuclear bombs*.
slides.sub: A B-52 on January 21, 1968, on the ice near the base. None detonated.
slides.image: Cracked sea ice glowing orange under a low arctic sun, ice in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain dark water, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: In 1946 the US offered *$100 million* in gold for the island.
slides.sub: Delivered December 14, 1946. Denmark declined a purchase, a 99-year lease and full US defence control.
slides.image: Stacked gold bars on a dark velvet cloth under warm light, bars in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain velvet, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: World's largest island, *56,000* people, 81% ice.
slides.sub: 2,166,086 km², capital Nuuk. Polls have shown about 85% of Greenlanders oppose an American takeover.
slides.image: A vast white ice sheet meeting dark rocky coast, seen from the air, ice in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain dark sea, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: Denmark sends *5.4 billion kroner* a year, over 20% of GDP.
slides.sub: About €724 million a year on average, 2019 to 2023. Home rule 1979, self-rule 2009, out of the EEC since 1985.
